name: Chloe Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in first-year business, and I live with my grandmother, Lola, in her flat in Marlow Park. I do reception at Luxe hair salon on Saturdays and two weekday afternoons. I book clients, answer the phone and sweep up. Evenings I'm either helping Lola with her shopping or working on my own project, an online shop selling hair accessories. I use AI every day for product descriptions and prices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the shop project.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started with fifty hair clips I bought wholesale, and I sold them on a marketplace site. Last month I made two hundred and ten pounds, minus costs about ninety. It's small, but it's mine. I believe in working for what you get, and I want to own a business like the salon owner, Mrs Delgado, who built hers from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine. The tools I use help a bit, but most things stay the same. I'd tell my friends that hard work still matters more than any technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay about AI, but my money is thin. I've got under a month saved, and the loan covers only fees. If Mrs Delgado cuts my afternoons, I lose a third of my income. Lola's pension helps with the rent, but I don't want to take from her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the salon job, keep growing the online shop, and put thirty pounds a month into savings. I'd add a second product line, maybe scrunchies, since they sell well. And I'd keep helping Lola with her shopping on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nothing scary, but money's always in the corner of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pressures would stay with you in an unchanged world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lola says to never spend what I haven't earned. She's right, but it's hard when the rent bill comes. I'd sell a few more items each month to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the salon cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to a local business meetup. There's one every month at the library, and the owners there give advice for free.

I'd say the tools I use help a bit and that's all.
think: My money is **thin**, under a month saved, with the loan covering fees only.
If Mrs Delgado cuts my afternoons I lose a **third** of my income.
do: Keep the salon job and keep **growing** the online shop.
Add a second **product line** like scrunchies.
Put thirty **pounds** a month into savings.
feel: **Uneasy**, with money always in the corner of my mind.
S0.quote: If Mrs Delgado cuts my afternoons, I lose a third of my income.
fieldNote: Comfortable with **AI**, so the plateau is a quiet worry about money.
Salon hours are her main exposure, along with a thin cushion.
Wants to earn, not take, which reflects her traditional values.

steps.text: Keep the salon reception shifts on Saturdays and two afternoons
Add scrunchies as a second product line in the online shop
Put thirty pounds a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for people who work. Tools make small businesses stronger if they're used well. I'd say that to Mrs Delgado, who's worried about the booking app taking her receptionist's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know my reception job is exactly what a booking app replaces. Answering phones, booking appointments, reminders. In a year or two, the salon might not need me. But my own shop gets stronger with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more cleverly, for pricing, photos and ads. I'd offer Mrs Delgado to set up the booking app for her, so I'm the person who knows it. I'd also grow the shop to five hundred pounds a month by next summer. And I'd keep the afternoons until the app takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's both a threat and an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would AI change a salon and your shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I set it up, I stay useful. She'd keep me on for the human bits, like greeting people and sorting out problems. A phone can't greet someone with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same to the other part-timers. Learn the tools before your boss decides without you.

I'd tell other part-timers to learn the tools **before the boss decides**.
think: My reception job is exactly what a **booking app** replaces.
My own shop gets **stronger** with the tools.
do: Offer to set up the **booking app** for Mrs Delgado.
Use the tools for **pricing**, photos and ads.
Grow the shop to five hundred **pounds** a month by summer.
feel: **Uneasy**, because it's both a threat and an opening.
S1.quote: A phone can't greet someone with a smile.
fieldNote: Sees her own **job** as the exposed one and acts to become the expert.
Her shop gains from the tools, so she's not purely threatened.
Shows leadership by warning other part-timers.

steps.text: Offer to set up the booking app for the salon
Use the tools for pricing, photos and ads in my shop
Grow the online shop to five hundred pounds a month by summer
Keep the salon afternoons until the app takes over

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep calm and keep working. I'd tell my friends that the ones who start something now will do better than the ones who wait. I'd also say government shouldn't clamp down in panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. If thinking work goes by 2028, a business degree and a reception job both go. My online shop is the same kind of thing, because anyone could make it. I'd have a thin cushion and a debt for a course that doesn't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on things AI can't do by 2031: people, trust, local things. I'd turn the shop into a local brand, with market stalls and delivery by hand. I'd cut my spending, and consider moving my studies part time. I'd ask Mrs Delgado to train me as a stylist, since that's hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep moving. Sitting still feels worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the business degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lola would say she lived through harder things. She'd say we've got each other and a roof. She'd make me eat, tell me to pray and keep working. That helps more than any advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lola think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also sell the idea to my friends. A market stall run by three of us could earn more than one online shop.

say: I'd say people who start something now will do **better** than those who wait.
I'd say governments shouldn't **clamp down** in panic.
think: A business degree and a **reception** job both go if thinking work goes by 2028.
Anyone could make my **online shop** too.
do: Turn the shop into a **local brand** with market stalls.
Ask Mrs Delgado to train me as a **stylist**.
Cut my **spending** and consider part-time study.
feel: **Anxious**, but moving, since sitting still feels worse.
S2.quote: I'd go hard on things AI can't do by 2031: people, trust, local things.
fieldNote: Her answer is to go **local and hands-on**, which fits the robot delay.
Admits fear but acts, in line with her adaptive trait.

steps.text: Take a market stall with two friends to sell hair accessories
Ask Mrs Delgado to train me as a stylist
Cut spending to rent share, food and stock
Move to part-time study to protect my income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window for people who act. I'd say to my friends, start your thing now and learn the tools. The ones who wait will regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel okay. By 2031 I'd be twenty-three with a few years of selling and a degree. I'd have a brand and some savings. Even if AGI arrives, a trusted local brand has value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, put aside a hundred pounds a month, and grow the shop into a proper small business with a stall, an online store and a few regular customers. I'd get a second product category, and learn accounting basics so I can handle the books myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd say excited too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you over two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a rush, five is a runway. The extra time means I can try, fail once, and fix it. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your business plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI arrives, I'd probably already be selling more to local people who want a person to deal with.

I'd tell friends to start their thing now and learn the **tools**.
think: By 2031 I'd have a **brand**, savings and a few years of selling.
A trusted **local brand** keeps value even if AGI arrives.
do: Put aside a hundred **pounds** a month.
Grow the shop into a **stall** plus an online store.
Learn **accounting** basics to handle my own books.
S3.quote: Two years is a rush, five is a runway. The extra time means I can try, fail once, and fix it.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan into a **runway** for trial and error.
Wants a local brand as a protection against AGI.
Adds accounting skills, practical and traditional.

steps.text: Put aside a hundred pounds a month
Open a weekend market stall alongside the online shop
Learn accounting basics through the degree to run my own books
Reinvest half of each month's profit in stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to build something real. I'd say it to the friends who feel doomed. We can plan and still be fine. I'd tell them to start small and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel good. By twenty-eight I could have my own shop or small brand, and a place of my own. If AGI comes, I'd be established, and used to the tools. I'm not afraid of change, I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, grow the business, and buy Lola a better chair. I'd save, invest in stock, and learn every new tool the day it comes out. I'd also hire a student part-time, the way Mrs Delgado hired me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can do things with this much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My future self would say thanks for starting early. I'd want her to have kept Lola comfortable, and to have had a dozen failed ideas and one good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your future self?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the kind of boss who trains people. That's what I'd like to hand on.

I'd tell doomed friends to start **small** and keep going.
think: By twenty-eight I could own a **shop** or small brand and a place of my own.
I'm not afraid of change, I **like it**.

feel: **Calm**, since this much time lets me do things.

fieldNote: Ten years makes her **calm** because her habits fit the change.
Values passing on opportunity, as Mrs Delgado did.
Cares about her grandmother's comfort as a goal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both my reception job and my business could be copied before I'm ready. What would help is time to build, cheap small-business advice, and a loan that waits if the business hasn't paid yet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that young people aren't asking for handouts. We want a fair start and room to work. Give us that and we'll build the rest.

headlineQuote: Young people aren't asking for handouts. We want a fair start and room to work.
portrait: Chloe is an eighteen-year-old **business** student who does salon reception and runs a small online hair accessories shop.
She lives with her grandmother, uses AI every day and believes in earning what you have.
Traditional and free-market in outlook, she responds to change by building and starting early.
Her own reception job is exposed, so she tries to become the person who sets the tools up.
She's **anxious** with two years and **calm** with ten, because time lets her build.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because her job and her shop could both be copied before she's ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Time** to build and cheap small-business advice.
A **loan** that waits if the business hasn't paid yet.
